v.why: With edge 0->3 already absent, removing 2->3 leaves only edge 4 to reach the output, so the cell can become disconnected or very weak (see experiments 3 and 95).
Replacing a parameter-free pool on the final edge with a learnable conv adds capacity to the output path, which gives large gains (see experiments 33 and 83).
If edge 2->3 is missing, adding 1->3 can reconnect the computation from node 1 to the output (see experiment 65).
When 2->3 is absent, a conv on the direct input->output edge may be the only effective learnable path (see experiment 96).
Without the direct 0->3 edge, adding a conv path through node 2 strongly improves connectivity and capacity (see experiment 76).
With edge 0->2 absent, removing 0->1 cuts off both intermediate nodes and leaves only edge 3 (see experiments 51 and 5).
Removing the direct edge when 2->3 is also absent leaves the output fed only by edge 4, which risks disconnection.
Swapping the strongest conv on the 0->2 edge for pooling removes key learnable capacity (see experiments 18 and 79).
Replacing a conv on the 1->2 edge with pooling loses capacity, whereas replacing none or skip there costs little (see experiment 16 compared with 35).
Deleting a 3x3 conv on the final edge removes the most valuable op on the output path, which hurts more than deleting skip or pool (see experiment 55 compared with 2).

raw:
Hypotheses from the 100 measured edits plus NAS-Bench-201 structure. Two mechanisms drive almost everything. First, a cell that loses its path to node 3, or keeps only parameter-free paths, collapses in accuracy. Second, replacing a convolution with pooling or `none` costs most when that convolution is the cell's main learnable path.
